content: Leukocytosis refers to an increase in the white blood cell (WBC) count above the normal range. While it can indicate an underlying illness, leukocytosis itself is not a disease or disorder but rather a laboratory finding. When the WBC count exceeds 25 to 30 x 10⁹/L, it is termed a leukemoid reaction. This reaction represents the response of a healthy bone marrow to significant stress, trauma, or infection. It is distinct from leukemia and leukoerythroblastosis, conditions in which immature blood cells are present in the peripheral blood. A WBC count of 8 x 10⁹/L or higher is generally indicative of leukocytosis. Leukocytosis is frequently observed in acutely ill patients and can result from a variety of conditions, including infections caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi, or parasites, as well as cancer, hemorrhage, and exposure to certain medications or chemicals, such as steroids. In some cases, leukocytosis may be the first indication of neoplastic growth involving leukocytes. For respiratory diseases like pneumonia and tuberculosis, the WBC count is a critical diagnostic parameter, as leukocytosis is commonly present in these conditions. The mechanisms underlying leukocytosis can take several forms. These include an increased release of leukocytes from the bone marrow storage pools, reduced margination of leukocytes along vessel walls, decreased extravasation of leukocytes from the bloodstream into tissues, or an increased production of precursor cells in the bone marrow. Leukocytosis can be classified based on the specific type of white blood cell that is elevated. When neutrophil counts are increased, the condition is referred to as neutrophilia. An elevated lymphocyte count is termed lymphocytosis. Similarly, an increase in monocyte count is called monocytosis, and a rise in eosinophil count is known as eosinophilia.
